error_modes.label: Altitude control through the lead change

texts.0: SP, due to a scan that stayed outside the cockpit on the other aircraft throughout the position swap, did not maintain the briefed formation altitude during the lead change. The aircraft departed the briefed altitude by more than 300 feet and the trend continued unchecked while the new position was being taken. The IP had to direct the correction and assist on the controls to re-establish the formation on the assigned altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed return of the instrument cross-check after acknowledging the lead change, allowed the aircraft to climb away from the briefed altitude. The deviation reached the 300 feet limit before it was arrested and was reduced only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP. Altitude was re-established late, after the new lead position had already been taken.
texts.2: SP, due to unintentional back pressure applied while accelerating into the lead position, allowed the aircraft to leave the briefed altitude. The excursion reached approximately 200 feet, between the 150 and 300 feet bands, before SP recognized the trend on the altimeter. The correction was made without prompting and the aircraft was re-established on altitude with no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained the briefed formation altitude throughout the lead change, keeping excursions inside 150 feet. Pitch inputs were small and were applied as soon as the trend appeared on the altimeter and the vertical speed indication. The transfer of the lead was completed with no degradation of altitude control.
texts.4: SP flew the lead change with altitude excursions of only a few tens of feet, well inside the 150 feet band. The instrument cross-check continued uninterrupted through the signal, the acknowledgement and the position swap. Altitude control was precise and no re-establishment was needed after the change.
texts.marginal: SP kept altitude within standards during the lead change, but the excursions repeatedly approached the 150 feet band and always in the same direction as power was increased to move forward. The corrections were correct in sense but were started only after the trend had developed. SP is expected to anticipate the pitch change associated with the power increase so that excursions remain clearly inside the band.

error_modes.label: Airspeed control during the position exchange

texts.0: SP, due to an uncontrolled power application used to move into the lead position, did not hold the briefed formation airspeed during the lead change. Airspeed varied by more than 20 knots from the briefed value and the closure with the other aircraft was not controlled. The IP had to intervene on the throttle and direct the re-establishment of the briefed airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to power changes made in large steps instead of small anticipated inputs, allowed airspeed to diverge from the briefed value while taking the lead. The deviation reached the 20 knots limit and was contained only after verbal prompting from the IP. Airspeed was stabilized late, after the formation had already settled in the new arrangement.
texts.2: SP, due to a power reduction applied late when the overtake was completed, allowed airspeed to build above the briefed value. The excursion reached about 15 knots, between the 10 and 20 knots bands, and was recognized by SP without prompting. Airspeed was returned to the briefed value promptly and no IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP controlled airspeed throughout the lead change and kept the deviation inside 10 knots of the briefed value. Power was set in small anticipated increments for the overtake and reduced in time to stop the acceleration in the new position. Closure with the other aircraft was managed without any airspeed excursion outside the band.
texts.4: SP flew the whole lead change with airspeed held within a few knots of the briefed value. Power was moved smoothly and led the required speed change rather than following it, so no correction was needed once the new position was taken. Closure and stabilization were both accomplished without any airspeed overshoot.
texts.marginal: SP kept airspeed within standards during the lead change, but each overtake ended close to the 10 knots band before the power reduction took effect. The technique met the criteria and the corrections were made without prompting, yet the margin available was consistently small. SP is expected to lead the power reduction so that the acceleration stops well inside the band.

error_modes.label: Exit heading on completion of the lead change

texts.0: SP, due to an uncoordinated roll input applied while stabilizing in the new position, did not establish the formation on the briefed heading on completion of the lead change. The heading error exceeded 10 degrees and the formation was left tracking away from the briefed direction with no correction started. The IP had to direct the turn back and supervise the recapture of the briefed heading.
texts.1: SP, due to a lookout that remained locked on the other aircraft after the swap, allowed the heading to drift away from the briefed exit heading. The error reached the 10 degrees limit and was corrected only after verbal prompting from the IP. The formation was re-established on the briefed heading well after the change was complete.
texts.2: SP, due to a small residual bank held while checking the position of the other aircraft, allowed the heading to move off the briefed exit heading. The error reached about 8 degrees, between the 5 and 10 degrees bands, and was identified by SP on the heading indication without prompting. SP corrected in time and no IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP established the formation on the briefed exit heading on completion of the lead change, with the error kept inside 5 degrees. The roll-out was coordinated and the heading was checked against the heading indication as soon as the new position was stable. No further correction was needed once the change was complete.
texts.4: SP rolled out of the lead change on the briefed exit heading with an error of one to two degrees. The heading was cross-checked during the swap rather than after it, so no recapture was required. The formation was stabilized on the briefed direction immediately after the exchange of positions.
texts.marginal: SP met the exit heading criteria after the lead change, but the roll-out consistently finished 4 to 5 degrees off the briefed heading before being trimmed back. The corrections were made without prompting and the standards were satisfied, however the initial accuracy of the roll-out was low. SP is expected to anticipate the roll-out point so that the heading is captured directly rather than recovered afterwards.

error_modes.label: Interpretation and acknowledgement of the lead change signal

texts.0: SP, due to non-standard phraseology that left the intention ambiguous, acted on the lead change signal without establishing what had actually been directed. The change was started in the wrong sense, neither aircraft was established as lead for several seconds and the briefed parameters were exceeded past the 20 knots and 10 degrees limits. The IP had to intervene, cancel the change and restore the briefed formation.
texts.1: SP, due to an acknowledgement that did not confirm the actual signal that had been passed, remained uncertain of the leader's intention after the visual signal was given. The change was started only after the signal had been repeated and after direct verbal prompting from the IP, with airspeed reaching the 20 knots limit during the delay. The correct sense of the change was finally established, but outside the briefed timing.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial misreading of the visual signal against the sun, hesitated at the start of the lead change. SP requested confirmation on the radio without any prompting, obtained it and executed the change in the correct sense, with the parameters staying between the code 3 and code 1 bands. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP identified the leader's verbal and visual signal for the lead change immediately and acknowledged it with standard phraseology. The change was executed in the correct sense and without misinterpretation, and the formation parameters remained inside the code 3 bands throughout the exchange.
texts.4: SP anticipated the lead change signal from the briefed sequence and recognized it at the moment it was passed, replying with concise standard phraseology. The exchange left no ambiguity between the two cockpits and the change followed immediately in the correct sense. Formation parameters showed negligible deviation across the whole exchange.
texts.marginal: SP interpreted the lead change signal correctly and executed it within standards, but the acknowledgement came after a noticeable pause and the first reply did not use the briefed wording. The criteria were met and the sense of the change was never in doubt. SP is expected to pre-arm the expected signal from the briefed sequence and to reply at once with standard phraseology.

error_modes.label: Assumption of formation leadership after the command

texts.0: SP, due to failure to exercise formation lead responsibilities after the lead change, did not assume leadership of the formation once the command had been received. No aircraft was setting the formation parameters or the navigation for a prolonged period, and airspeed and heading moved beyond the 20 knots and 10 degrees limits. The IP had to take the lead role and direct the recovery of the formation.
texts.1: SP, due to hesitation in taking up the lead responsibilities that had just been handed over, continued to fly as the wingman after receiving the command. The lead was assumed only after a second instruction and repeated verbal prompting, with heading reaching the 10 degrees limit while no aircraft was setting the direction. The formation was re-established late and only under the IP's direction.
texts.2: SP, due to an incomplete transfer of attention from wingman duties to lead duties, was slow to start setting the formation parameters after taking the lead. Airspeed and heading drifted to values between the code 3 and code 1 bands before SP recognized the omission. SP then set and held the briefed parameters without any IP intervention.
texts.3: SP assumed formation leadership without uncertainty as soon as the command was received. The briefed airspeed, altitude and heading were set and held from the moment of the transfer, and the wingman was given a stable platform to fly on. Parameters remained inside the code 3 bands throughout.
texts.4: SP took over formation leadership the instant the command was received and flew the formation with parameters that were both stable and smooth from the first seconds. Power and attitude changes were small enough to keep the wingman comfortably in position. Deviations from the briefed parameters were negligible for the whole period in the lead.
texts.marginal: SP assumed formation leadership within standards after the command, but for the first seconds the parameters were set reactively rather than deliberately and drifted toward the middle of the band. Leadership was never in doubt and no prompting was required. SP is expected to establish and announce the briefed parameters immediately on taking the lead so that the wingman has a stable reference from the outset.

error_modes.label: Safe separation and mutual visual contact during the swap

texts.0: SP, due to an excessive rate of closure while moving forward into the lead position, did not execute the lead change safely. Lateral separation reduced below the briefed value and the other aircraft passed out of sight in the forward hemisphere for part of the movement. The IP had to intervene on the controls to restore separation and stop the maneuver.
texts.1: SP, due to a movement started before the lateral displacement had been established, executed the lead change with the two aircraft closer than the briefed separation. The geometry was opened out only after the IP called for more spacing, and airspeed reached the 20 knots limit while the correction was made. Visual contact with the other aircraft was maintained, but the margins used were the minimum acceptable.
texts.2: SP, due to a lateral displacement that was slightly less than briefed at the start of the swap, allowed the separation to reduce during the overtake. SP recognized the closure early, stopped the forward movement and re-opened the geometry, with the parameters remaining between the code 3 and code 1 bands. Visual contact was continuous and no IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP executed the lead change safely, establishing the briefed lateral displacement before starting the forward movement and keeping the other aircraft in sight throughout. Closure was controlled and the separation never reduced below the briefed value. The exchange of positions was completed with all parameters inside the code 3 bands.
texts.4: SP set up the lead change with clear lateral displacement, maintained uninterrupted visual contact with the other aircraft and controlled the closure so that the swap looked deliberate at every stage. Separation stayed comfortably above the briefed minimum from start to finish. The whole maneuver was flown with negligible deviation from the briefed parameters.
texts.marginal: SP executed the lead change with safe separation, but the lateral displacement established before the forward movement was consistently at the low end of the briefed spacing. Visual contact was maintained and no correction was needed from the IP. SP is expected to build in a larger initial displacement so that the safety margin does not depend on precise closure control.

error_modes.label: Compliance with the published and ATC restrictions for lead change

texts.0: SP, due to lack of awareness of a published restriction that was available in the briefing material, carried out the lead change outside the conditions permitted by B.O 3-1 and the ATC clearance in force. The change was made in an area and at a level where it was not authorized, and altitude was allowed to deviate by more than 300 feet while the geometry was sorted out. The IP had to stop the maneuver, restore the cleared profile and coordinate with ATC.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete review of the restrictions applicable to the lead change, started the exchange before the conditions required by B.O 3-1 and by the ATC clearance were satisfied. The maneuver was suspended and repositioned only after the IP pointed out the restriction, and altitude reached the 300 feet limit during the interruption. Compliance was finally achieved, but only after direct prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a late check of the clearance limits against the planned lead change point, began setting up the exchange slightly early with respect to the applicable restriction. SP recognized the discrepancy without prompting, delayed the change until the restriction was satisfied and kept the parameters between the code 3 and code 1 bands during the delay. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP complied with the restrictions of B.O 3-1 and with the ATC clearance for the lead change. The applicable conditions were checked before the exchange was set up and the maneuver was carried out only inside the authorized area and level block. Formation parameters were held inside the code 3 bands during the whole sequence.
texts.4: SP had the applicable B.O 3-1 and ATC restrictions identified before the exchange and confirmed the clearance limits without any interruption of the formation task. The lead change was executed inside the authorized boundaries with no doubt at any moment about its legality. Parameter deviations during the sequence were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP complied with the B.O 3-1 and ATC restrictions for the lead change, but the applicable limits were confirmed only shortly before the exchange rather than during the planning of the sequence. No restriction was infringed and no prompting was needed. SP is expected to confirm the applicable restrictions early enough that the decision to change lead is never made under time pressure.

error_modes.label: Execution of the lead change at the briefed point and per SOP

texts.0: SP, due to an unmonitored position relative to the sequence agreed at the pre-flight briefing, did not perform the lead change at the point determined in the briefing or in the manner set out in the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the SOPs. The exchange was started at an arbitrary point in the profile and the sequence of actions did not follow the briefed pattern, with heading and airspeed diverging past the 10 degrees and 20 knots limits. The IP had to stop the maneuver and re-brief the sequence in flight.
texts.1: SP, due to a mental picture of the sortie that had not been updated after the previous turn, arrived at the briefed lead change point without being ready to execute. The exchange was carried out well past the briefed point and only after the IP prompted for it, with airspeed at the 20 knots limit while SP caught up with the sequence. The steps of the procedure were completed, but out of the briefed order.
texts.2: SP, due to attention held on the geometry of the formation, was late in recognizing the arrival at the briefed lead change point. SP identified the omission without prompting, executed the exchange shortly after the briefed point and followed the sequence of the Techniques and Procedures Manual, with parameters staying between the code 3 and code 1 bands. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP performed the lead change at the point determined during the pre-flight briefing and in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the SOPs. The signal, the acknowledgement and the exchange of positions followed the briefed order without omissions. Formation parameters remained inside the code 3 bands for the whole sequence.
texts.4: SP arrived at the briefed lead change point already configured and positioned for the exchange, and executed it exactly as set out in the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the SOPs. The sequence ran without hesitation or repeated actions and the timing matched the pre-flight briefing precisely. Deviations from the briefed parameters were negligible throughout.
texts.marginal: SP executed the lead change at the briefed point and in the briefed order, but the preparation for it began only at the point itself rather than in advance, so the first actions were rushed. The procedure was completed correctly and within standards. SP is expected to anticipate the arrival at the briefed point so that the exchange is set up before it is reached.

error_modes.label: Position relative to the 3/9 line when the lead is taken

texts.0: SP, due to disregard of the requirement to be on or forward of the 3/9 line before taking the lead, assumed formation leadership while still well aft of the 3/9 line of the other aircraft. The formation was led from a position from which the new leader could neither see nor clear for the wingman, and airspeed and heading were allowed to diverge past the 20 knots and 10 degrees limits while the geometry was sorted out. The IP had to intervene, hand the lead back and direct the repositioning forward of the 3/9 line before the change was repeated.
texts.1: SP, due to an overtake that was started without a check of the position relative to the 3/9 line, acknowledged the lead change and began acting as leader while still aft of the 3/9 line. The forward movement to the required position was made only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP, and airspeed reached the 20 knots limit during the late overtake. The lead was eventually held from a correct position, but only after direct intervention by voice.
texts.2: SP, due to a late start of the forward movement after the signal, was still short of the 3/9 line when the lead was accepted. SP recognized the position error without prompting, completed the overtake to line abreast and stabilized there, with airspeed reaching about 15 knots off the briefed value between the 10 and 20 knots bands. No IP intervention was required at any stage of the exchange.
texts.3: SP established the aircraft on or forward of the 3/9 line before taking the lead, as required for the transfer of leadership. The overtake to the line abreast route position was completed before the lead was accepted and airspeed and heading stayed inside the 10 knots and 5 degrees bands. The position from which the formation was led allowed the wingman to be seen and cleared for at all times.
texts.4: SP moved to a position clearly forward of the 3/9 line before accepting the lead, so leadership was never taken from a position aft of the wingman. The overtake was flown with airspeed and heading deviations of only a few units and the line abreast picture was held steady on arrival. The transfer of leadership took effect with the correct geometry already established.
texts.marginal: SP took the lead from a position on the 3/9 line rather than forward of it, so the requirement was met only marginally on each attempt. The overtake was completed without prompting and the parameters stayed inside the bands throughout. SP is expected to move clearly forward of the 3/9 line before accepting the lead so that the required position does not depend on an exact judgement of the abeam picture.

error_modes.label: Expeditious execution of a lead change made with visual signals

texts.0: SP, due to a slow lead change with visual signals, extended the period during which no aircraft was actively clearing for the formation. The exchange of positions dragged on with repeated signals and no leader setting the parameters, and altitude and heading were allowed to move past the 300 feet and 10 degrees limits while the formation drifted. The IP had to intervene, complete the transfer by radio and re-establish the briefed profile.
texts.1: SP, due to hesitation between the visual signal and the movement into position, allowed the lead change to take much longer than the briefed sequence required. The formation flew for an extended period without a leader actively clearing for it and the exchange was closed out only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP, with heading reaching the 10 degrees limit. The correct positions were finally established, but well outside the intended timing.
texts.2: SP, due to a visual signal that was answered before the following actions had been prepared, executed the lead change more slowly than the technique requires. The period without a leader clearing for the formation was longer than briefed and heading drifted about 8 degrees, between the 5 and 10 degrees bands, before SP closed the sequence out without prompting. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP executed the lead change with visual signals expeditiously, so that the time without a leader actively clearing for the formation was kept to a minimum. The signal, the head nod and the movement into position followed each other without dead time and the parameters stayed inside the 150 feet and 5 degrees bands. Clearing responsibility was picked up by the new leader as soon as the exchange was complete.
texts.4: SP ran the visual lead change through to completion without any pause between the signal, the acknowledgement and the change of positions. The formation was without an actively clearing leader for no more than the few seconds inherent in the technique, and the deviations from the briefed parameters were negligible. Clearing was resumed by the new leader immediately after the transfer.
texts.marginal: SP completed the visual lead change within standards, but each step was started only after the previous one had fully finished, so the total time without a leader clearing for the formation was at the upper end of what is acceptable. No prompting was needed and the parameters remained inside the bands. SP is expected to overlap the acknowledgement with the movement into position so that the exchange stays clearly expeditious.

error_modes.label: Treating the lead change as complete before it is acknowledged

texts.0: SP, due to considering the lead change complete before the other aircraft had acknowledged it, stopped exercising the responsibilities of the position while the other aircraft had not yet taken them up. Both cockpits acted for a prolonged period on the assumption that the other one was leading, and airspeed and heading were allowed to exceed the 20 knots and 10 degrees limits with no aircraft setting the formation parameters. The IP had to intervene, state who was leading and restore the briefed formation.
texts.1: SP, due to a transfer that was treated as effective on transmission rather than on acknowledgement, released the duties of the position before any acknowledgement had been received. The ambiguity persisted until the IP prompted verbally for a positive confirmation, and by then heading had reached the 10 degrees limit. The correct assignment of the lead was re-established only after that prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to an assumption that the lead change had been taken up as soon as the signal was passed, was slow to notice that no acknowledgement had been received. SP recognized the missing acknowledgement without prompting, requested it on the radio and confirmed the transfer, with the parameters staying between the code 3 and code 1 bands during the short period of doubt. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP considered the lead change complete only after the acknowledgement had been received, so the responsibilities of the two positions were never in doubt. The duties of the previous position were carried on until the acknowledgement arrived and the parameters were held inside the 150 feet and 5 degrees bands during the exchange. The transfer was clearly understood by both aircraft.
texts.4: SP treated the transfer as effective at the exact moment the acknowledgement was received, neither earlier nor later, so responsibilities passed cleanly from one aircraft to the other. There was no interval in which the lead was ambiguous and the formation parameters showed negligible deviation. The change of duties was evident to both cockpits without further discussion.
texts.marginal: SP waited for the acknowledgement before treating the lead change as complete, but on more than one occasion the handover of duties began a moment before the acknowledgement was fully read back. The transfer was never actually ambiguous and no prompting was required. SP is expected to hold the responsibilities of the position until the acknowledgement is complete so that no interval exists in which the lead is assumed rather than confirmed.

error_modes.label: Movement to route line abreast before the lead is transferred

texts.0: SP, due to omission of the directed move from fingertip to route position, attempted to exchange the lead directly from close formation. The overtake was flown from fingertip spacing without the line abreast picture ever being established, and altitude and airspeed were allowed to diverge past the 300 feet and 20 knots limits during the crossing movement. The IP had to intervene on the controls, open the formation out and stop the exchange.
texts.1: SP, due to a move to route position that was started but not completed before the exchange, began taking the lead from spacing that was still inside route. The formation was opened to the required line abreast position only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP, and airspeed reached the 20 knots limit while the geometry was corrected. The exchange was completed correctly, but only after direct prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a lateral movement that lagged behind the direction to route, arrived at the line abreast position later than the technique requires. SP recognized the delay without prompting, completed the move to the route line abreast picture and only then took the lead, with the parameters staying between the code 3 and code 1 bands. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP moved from fingertip to the route line abreast position in wings level flight before the lead was transferred, as directed. The spacing and the abeam line were established before the exchange and altitude and airspeed remained inside the 150 feet and 10 knots bands. The transfer was then carried out from the correct formation position.
texts.4: SP established the route line abreast position promptly and precisely as soon as it was directed, so the lead change started from exactly the geometry the technique calls for. The move out of fingertip was flown in wings level flight with negligible deviation in altitude and airspeed. The exchange followed from a stable and clearly defined position.
texts.marginal: SP moved to route before the lead was transferred, but the spacing established was at the inner edge of route and the abeam line was still being corrected when the exchange began. The standards were met and no prompting was needed. SP is expected to settle the route line abreast picture fully before starting the transfer so that the position is unambiguous at the moment the lead changes.

error_modes.label: Power setting established by the new leader for the rejoining wingman

texts.0: SP, due to failure to establish a power setting that would aid the new Number 2 in moving to the proper position, flew the lead with continuously varying power immediately after taking it. The other aircraft was left without a stable platform to move on, could not achieve the briefed position and the airspeed of the formation varied by more than 20 knots. The IP had to intervene, set and call a fixed power setting and stabilize the formation.
texts.1: SP, due to power changes that continued after the lead had been assumed, did not give the new Number 2 a stable reference for taking up position. The setting was frozen only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP and the airspeed of the formation reached the 20 knots limit while the wingman was still moving. The position was eventually taken, but late and with an unnecessarily large power correction by the wingman.
texts.2: SP, due to a power setting that was chosen only after the lead had already been taken, made the first part of the wingman's movement to position harder than necessary. Airspeed varied by about 15 knots, between the 10 and 20 knots bands, before SP recognized the effect and stabilized the setting without prompting. The wingman then achieved the proper position with no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP established a power setting on assuming the lead that aided the new Number 2 in moving to the proper position. The setting was held steady while the other aircraft repositioned and the airspeed of the formation stayed inside the 10 knots band. The wingman was able to take up the briefed position with small corrections only.
texts.4: SP set a stable power setting at the moment the lead was assumed and held it unchanged until the new Number 2 was established in position. The airspeed of the formation varied by only a few knots and the wingman moved into position without having to chase the leader. The platform offered to the wingman was steady from the first seconds of the new arrangement.
texts.marginal: SP established a power setting for the new Number 2 within standards, but it was adjusted more than once while the wingman was still moving to position. The airspeed stayed inside the band and the wingman achieved position without prompting. SP is expected to select the setting deliberately at the moment of the transfer and to leave it untouched until the wingman is stable in the briefed position.

error_modes.label: Choice of radio instead of visual signals when visibility is limited

texts.0: SP, due to persistence with visual signals when limited visibility made them unreadable, attempted to transfer the lead by a method that could not work in the prevailing conditions. The signal was neither seen nor acknowledged, the formation continued with the lead undefined and altitude and heading were allowed to exceed the 300 feet and 10 degrees limits. The IP had to intervene, execute the change on the radio and re-establish the briefed profile.
texts.1: SP, due to repeated attempts to pass a visual signal in conditions of reduced visibility, delayed the lead change well past the briefed point. The radio was used only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP and heading reached the 10 degrees limit during the period without a defined leader. The change was finally completed correctly, but only after that prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial visual signal attempted in marginal visibility, lost time before recognizing that the method was unsuitable. SP switched to the radio without prompting and completed the exchange, with heading drifting about 8 degrees, between the 5 and 10 degrees bands, during the delay. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP recognized that visibility was limited and used the radio to execute the lead change, as the technique directs. The transfer was passed and acknowledged on the first call and the formation parameters were kept inside the 150 feet and 5 degrees bands. The method chosen matched the conditions and left no ambiguity between the aircraft.
texts.4: SP assessed the visibility before the exchange and elected to use the radio from the outset, so no time was lost on a signal that could not have been read. The lead change was passed, acknowledged and completed in a single exchange with negligible deviation from the briefed parameters. The choice of method was made in advance rather than after a failed attempt.
texts.marginal: SP used the radio for the lead change in limited visibility as required, but the decision to do so was made only after a visual signal had first been considered and started. The exchange was completed within standards and without prompting. SP is expected to assess the visibility early enough that the method of transfer is selected before the change is initiated.

error_modes.label: Lead responsibilities after the lead change of the battle damage check

texts.0: SP, due to attention held on the aircraft being inspected after taking the lead for the second half of the battle damage check, did not clear for the flight or maintain radio responsibility while in the lead position. The formation was flown for a prolonged period with nobody clearing or answering, and altitude and heading were allowed to exceed the 300 feet and 10 degrees limits. The IP had to take over the lead duties, restore the clearing pattern and stop the check.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete pick-up of lead duties on assuming lead for the battle damage check, continued to concentrate on the inspecting aircraft instead of clearing for the flight and complying with the clearance in force. The lead duties were taken up only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP and heading reached the 10 degrees limit in the meantime. Radio responsibility was resumed late, after the inspection had already begun.
texts.2: SP, due to a divided scan between the inspecting aircraft and the flight path after the lead change of the battle damage check, was slow to start clearing for the formation. Heading and altitude drifted to values between the code 3 and code 1 bands before SP recognized the omission without prompting and resumed the lead duties. Clearing and radio responsibility were then maintained with no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP assumed the lead for the battle damage check and cleared for the flight, complied with the clearance in force and maintained radio responsibility while being inspected. The flight path was flown steadily so the inspecting aircraft could work, and altitude and heading stayed inside the 150 feet and 5 degrees bands. The check was completed with the lead duties fully covered throughout.
texts.4: SP took the lead for the battle damage check and covered clearing, clearance compliance and radio responsibility without any prompting from the moment of the transfer. The flight path offered to the inspecting aircraft was steady enough for the inspection to be completed in one pass, with negligible deviation in altitude and heading. Lead duties were never interrupted by the inspection itself.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the lead duties during the battle damage check within standards, but the clearing scan was interrupted each time the inspecting aircraft moved across the canopy. No omission developed into a deviation and no prompting was required. SP is expected to keep the clearing pattern and the radio watch independent of the movement of the inspecting aircraft.

error_modes.label: Lead change offered and taken when an emergency is being carried

texts.0: SP, due to failure to apply the rule that the aircraft with the malfunction should be given the Number 1 position, continued the sortie in the Number 2 position while carrying an emergency and closer than route formation. The aircraft with the malfunction was left flying formation instead of handling the problem, and altitude and airspeed were allowed to exceed the 300 feet and 20 knots limits while attention was split. The IP had to intervene, call Knock It Off, execute the lead change and open the formation.
texts.1: SP, due to hesitation over accepting the Number 1 position when it was offered after the malfunction, remained as Number 2 with the emergency and inside route spacing. The lead was taken and the spacing opened only after the offer had been repeated and after direct verbal prompting from the IP, with airspeed reaching the 20 knots limit during the delay. The correct arrangement was eventually established, but late in the recovery.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed decision when the Number 1 position was offered at the time the malfunction occurred, kept the wingman role for longer than the situation warranted. SP accepted the position at the next offer without prompting, opened the spacing to no closer than route and handled the malfunction, with the parameters staying between the code 3 and code 1 bands during the exchange. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP took the Number 1 position when it was offered after the malfunction, so the aircraft with the emergency was no longer required to maintain formation position. The spacing was kept no closer than route while the emergency was handled and altitude and airspeed remained inside the 150 feet and 10 knots bands. Communication and navigation for the flight were carried by the aircraft in the lead throughout.
texts.4: SP accepted the Number 1 position at the first offer, called Knock It Off and informed the other aircraft of the problem, the intentions and the assistance required. The lead change was completed without any interruption to the handling of the malfunction and the parameters showed negligible deviation. The recovery was led from the front with spacing that stayed well outside route at all times.
texts.marginal: SP took the Number 1 position when it was offered while carrying the malfunction, but the decision followed a period of consideration and the spacing was opened only to the edge of route. The standards were met and no prompting was needed. SP is expected to accept the lead at the first offer and to open the spacing clearly beyond route so that the emergency can be handled without any formation task.
